final_proof:
Put
\[
H=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(F-,-),\qquad K=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(-,G-),
\]
regarded as functors \(\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathbf C\to\mathbf{Set}\). We show that the two definitions specify exactly the same data.

First make the variance convention explicit. An arrow \(f^{\mathrm{op}}:D_1^{\mathrm{op}}\to D_2^{\mathrm{op}}\) in \(\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}}\) corresponds to an arrow \(f:D_2\to D_1\) in \(\mathbf D\). Thus, if \(g:C_1\to C_2\), the arrow
\[
(f^{\mathrm{op}},g):(D_1^{\mathrm{op}},C_1)\to(D_2^{\mathrm{op}},C_2)
\]
is carried by \(H\) and \(K\), respectively, to
\[
H(f^{\mathrm{op}},g)(h)=g\circ h\circ Ff\qquad(h:FD_1\to C_1)
\]
and
\[
K(f^{\mathrm{op}},g)(k)=Gg\circ k\circ f\qquad(k:D_1\to GC_1).
\]
These compositions are well typed because \(Ff:FD_2\to FD_1\) and \(Gg:GC_1\to GC_2\).

Assume Definition 1. The natural isomorphism \(\alpha:H\Rightarrow K\) has, at each object \((D^{\mathrm{op}},C)\), a component
\[
\alpha_{(D^{\mathrm{op}},C)}:\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(FD,C)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(D,GC).
\]
Every component of a natural isomorphism is an isomorphism in its codomain category; an isomorphism in \(\mathbf{Set}\) is a bijection. For the arrow \((f^{\mathrm{op}},g)\), naturality says
\[
K(f^{\mathrm{op}},g)\circ\alpha_{(D_1^{\mathrm{op}},C_1)}
=
\alpha_{(D_2^{\mathrm{op}},C_2)}\circ H(f^{\mathrm{op}},g). \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, applying the two sides of (1) to an arbitrary \(h:FD_1\to C_1\) gives, respectively,
\[
Gg\circ\alpha_{(D_1^{\mathrm{op}},C_1)}(h)\circ f
\]
and
\[
\alpha_{(D_2^{\mathrm{op}},C_2)}(g\circ h\circ Ff).
\]
Their equality is exactly the commutative-square equation required in Definition 2, with the sides interchanged. Thus Definition 1 implies Definition 2.

Conversely, assume Definition 2. Use its stated bijections as the components of a family \(\alpha:H\Rightarrow K\). For every arrow \((f^{\mathrm{op}},g)\) and every \(h:FD_1\to C_1\), the required equation is
\[
\alpha_{(D_2^{\mathrm{op}},C_2)}(g\circ h\circ Ff)
=
Gg\circ\alpha_{(D_1^{\mathrm{op}},C_1)}(h)\circ f. \tag{2}
\]
By the two action formulas above, (2) is the pointwise equality
\[
\alpha_{(D_2^{\mathrm{op}},C_2)}\circ H(f^{\mathrm{op}},g)
=
K(f^{\mathrm{op}},g)\circ\alpha_{(D_1^{\mathrm{op}},C_1)}.
\]
Since this holds for every arrow in \(\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathbf C\), the family \(\alpha\) is a natural transformation \(H\Rightarrow K\).

It remains to show that it is a natural isomorphism. Each component is a bijection by hypothesis, so define
\[
\beta_{(D^{\mathrm{op}},C)}=\alpha_{(D^{\mathrm{op}},C)}^{-1}.
\]
For an arrow \(u=(f^{\mathrm{op}},g)\), abbreviate the components at its source and target by \(\alpha_1,\alpha_2\), and put \(\beta_i=\alpha_i^{-1}\). Naturality of \(\alpha\) says
\[
\alpha_2H(u)=K(u)\alpha_1.
\]
Composing on the left with \(\beta_2\) and on the right with \(\beta_1\) gives
\[
H(u)\beta_1=\beta_2K(u),
\]
which is the naturality equation for \(\beta:K\Rightarrow H\). Componentwise, \(\beta\alpha\) and \(\alpha\beta\) are identity maps. Hence \(\beta\) is a natural inverse of \(\alpha\), so \(\alpha\) is a natural isomorphism. This is Definition 1.

Therefore Definitions 1 and 2 are equivalent.
